newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African committee to probe non-voting "N" shares.
newsitem.headline: S.African committee to probe non-voting "N" shares.

text.p: South Africa's Department of Trade and Industry said on Wednesday that the Standing Advisory Committee on Company Law was seeking public comment as to whether "N" shares should be outlawed.
"N" shares carry negligible voting rights so that, in most cases, they are effectively non-voting.
The closing date for submissions to the committee is August 31, 1997.
The DTI said the listing of "N" shares by South African companies was clearly designed to entrench control.

It noted that Johannesburg Stock Exchange rules required shareholders other than the controlling shareholder to also approve the creation of "N" shares which should, in theory, prevent them being forced on minorities.
But it added: "In practice, a large number of investors are quite happy to let management do what management does best."
The DTI said it wanted to make the investing public aware of the risks involved in "N" shares, as well as seeking public comment on whether they should continue to be allowed.
"N" shares have proved controversial in South Africa since new listing requirements opened the door to limited voting right shares in 1995.

Critics, including the Shareholders Association of South Africa, argue that the practice is frowned on by most international exchanges and is primarily aimed at preventing hostile takeovers which may well be in the best interests of minority shareholders.
